text: Definition 1 (weak proximal oracle) . A map $\mathcal{A}:\mathbb{V}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow\mathop{\mbox{\rm dom}}(\mathcal{R})$ is called a weak proximal oracle for Problem ( 1 ) if, for every ${\mathbf{y}}\in\mathbb{V}$ and $\lambda>0$ , it outputs a point ${\mathbf{x}}\in\mathop{\mbox{\rm dom}}(\mathcal{R})$ such that for any ${\mathbf{x}}^{*}\in\mathcal{X}^{*}$ , $\displaystyle\lambda\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}-{\mathbf{y}}\right\rVert^{2}+\mathcal{R}({\mathbf{x}})\leq\lambda\left\lVert{\mathbf{x}}^{*}-{\mathbf{y}}\right\rVert^{2}+\mathcal{R}({\mathbf{x}}^{*}).$ (4)

Definition 2 (restricted proximal oracle) . Let $\widehat{\mathcal{K}}\subseteq\mathop{\mbox{\rm dom}}(\mathcal{R})$ be a closed, but not necessarily convex, set satisfying $\mathcal{X}^{*}\subseteq\widehat{\mathcal{K}}$ . A map $\mathcal{A}:\mathbb{V}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}\rightarrow\widehat{\mathcal{K}}$ is called a restricted proximal oracle associated with $\widehat{\mathcal{K}}$ if, for every ${\mathbf{y}}\in\mathbb{V}$ and $\lambda>0$ , it outputs a point in $\displaystyle\argmin_{{\mathbf{z}}\in\widehat{\mathcal{K}}}\left\{\lambda\left\lVert{\mathbf{z}}-{\mathbf{y}}\right\rVert^{2}+\mathcal{R}({\mathbf{z}})\right\}.$ (5) Since $\mathcal{X}^{*}\subseteq\widehat{\mathcal{K}}$ , every restricted proximal oracle is a weak proximal oracle in the sense of Definition 1 .

Definition 3 ( $k$ -fold sparse projection oracle) . Suppose $\mathcal{R}$ is the indicator function of a convex and compact set $\mathcal{K}\subset\mathbb{V}$ whose set of vertices is denoted $\mathcal{V}$ . Suppose every ${\mathbf{x}}^{*}\in\mathcal{X}^{*}$ can be written as a convex combination of at most $s$ vertices from $\mathcal{V}$ , where $s<<n$ . For a positive integer $k$ such that $ks\leq n$ , a $k$ -fold sparse projection oracle is an oracle that for every ${\mathbf{y}}\in\mathbb{V}$ , outputs a point in $\displaystyle\argmin_{{\mathbf{z}}\in\mathcal{C}_{sk}}\left\lVert{\mathbf{z}}-{\mathbf{y}}\right\rVert,$ (6) where $\mathcal{C}_{sk}\subseteq\mathcal{K}$ contains all points in $\mathcal{K}$ that can be written as the convex combination of at most $s\cdot{}k$ vertices from $\mathcal{V}$ . In particular, this oracle implements the restricted proximal oracle of Definition 2 with $\widehat{\mathcal{K}}=\mathcal{C}_{sk}$ .

Theorem 1 (Deterministic geometric lower bound) . Fix an integer $N\geq 5$ , $1\leq k\leq 6N$ , and $R>0$ . For every deterministic method making at most $T\leq\lfloor N/(4k)\rfloor$ projections onto $\mathcal{C}_{k}$ (see ( 7 )), there exist orthonormal vectors ${\mathbf{q}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbf{q}}_{N}\in\mathbb{R}^{2N}$ , a unit vector ${\mathbf{r}}\in\mathbb{R}^{2N}$ , and a deterministic tie-breaking rule for the projection oracle such that, for the resulting set $\mathcal{K}_{N,R}\subset\mathbb{R}^{6N}$ defined by ( 9 ), the method returns either an infeasible point or a point $\widehat{\mathbf{w}}$ satisfying $\displaystyle\left\lVert\widehat{\mathbf{w}}-{\mathbf{s}}^{*}\right\rVert^{2}\geq\frac{R^{2}}{2}.$ Between sparse-projection calls, the method may also receive arbitrary answers from auxiliary oracles whose response rules do not depend on ${\mathbf{q}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbf{q}}_{N}$ or ${\mathbf{r}}$ . In the applications below, these auxiliary answers are precisely the free first-order oracle answers.

Theorem 2 (The nonsmooth case) . Fix $\alpha,G>0$ , an integer $N\geq 5$ , and $1\leq k\leq 6N$ . For every deterministic method using at most $\lfloor N/(4k)\rfloor$ calls to a $k$ -fold sparse projection oracle, there exists an instance in dimension $n=6N$ with compact feasible set, an $\alpha$ -strongly convex objective whose feasible subgradients have norm at most $G$ , and a unique vertex minimizer, such that the returned point $\widehat{\mathbf{w}}$ is either infeasible or $\displaystyle f(\widehat{\mathbf{w}})-f({\mathbf{w}}^{*})\geq\frac{G^{2}}{36\alpha N}.$ (14) Arbitrarily many first-order calls between sparse projections are allowed. Consequently, there is a universal constant $c_{0}>0$ such that, whenever $G^{2}/(\alpha\epsilon{}k)$ is sufficiently large, every deterministic method that guarantees an $\epsilon$ -optimal feasible point on all such instances requires at least $c_{0}G^{2}/(\alpha\epsilon k)$ $k$ -fold sparse projections in the worst case.

Remark 1 . Note that the bounded-subgradient property in Theorem 2 holds on more than just the feasible set. Indeed, $\mathcal{K}_{N,R}\subseteq\{{\mathbf{w}}:\left\lVert{\mathbf{w}}\right\rVert\leq R\}$ , and for every $\left\lVert{\mathbf{w}}\right\rVert\leq R$ and every ${\mathbf{g}}\in\partial f({\mathbf{w}})$ , $\left\lVert{\mathbf{g}}\right\rVert\leq\alpha R+\frac{2G}{3}=\frac{G}{3\sqrt{N}}+\frac{2G}{3}\leq G.$ Thus the lower bound continues to hold when subgradients are assumed bounded on a Euclidean ball containing the feasible set. This is the same type of neighborhood-access assumption used by MOPES [ 18 ] to obtain its improved projection complexity for nonsmooth constrained optimization.

Theorem 3 (The smooth case) . Fix $\alpha,\beta>0$ , let $\kappa:=\beta/\alpha$ , $N:=\left\lfloor(\kappa-5)/16\right\rfloor$ , and suppose that $\kappa\geq 85$ . For every $1\leq k\leq 6N$ and every deterministic method using at most $\lfloor N/(4k)\rfloor$ calls to a $k$ -fold sparse projection oracle, there exists an instance in dimension $n=6N$ with an $\alpha$ -strongly convex and $\beta$ -smooth quadratic objective, a unique vertex minimizer, and a feasible set diameter $D$ satisfying $D\leq 2$ , such that the returned point $\widehat{{\mathbf{w}}}$ is either infeasible or $\displaystyle f(\widehat{\mathbf{w}})-f({\mathbf{w}}^{*})\geq\frac{\alpha}{4}.$ (16) Consequently, for $\epsilon=\alpha/8$ , every deterministic method that guarantees an $\epsilon$ -optimal feasible point on all such instances requires $\Omega\left(\beta/(\alpha k)\right)$ calls to the $k$ -fold sparse projection oracle in worst case.

Theorem 4 (Randomized geometric lower bound) . For any $N\geq 8$ , let $T\leq\left\lfloor N/(128\log(2N))\right\rfloor$ . Every randomized method using at most $T$ calls to a $1$ -fold sparse projection oracle, while making arbitrary first-order calls whose returned answers are generated by a rule independent of $\sigma$ , has some fixed $\sigma\in\{-1,+1\}^{N}$ for which its output $\widehat{\mathbf{w}}=(\widehat{\mathbf{x}},\widehat{\mathbf{z}})$ satisfies $\mathbb{E}\left\lVert\widehat{\mathbf{x}}-R{\mathbf{u}}_{\sigma}\right\rVert^{2}\geq\frac{R^{2}}{4},$ where the expectation is taken over the internal randomness of the method.

Theorem 5 (The nonsmooth case) . Fix $\alpha,G>0$ and an integer $N\geq 8$ . For every randomized method using at most $\lfloor N/(128\log(2N))\rfloor$ calls to a $1$ -fold sparse-projection oracle, there exists an instance in dimension $n=2N$ with compact feasible set, an $\alpha$ -strongly convex objective whose feasible subgradients have norm at most $G$ , and a unique vertex minimizer ${\mathbf{w}}^{*}$ , such that $\mathbb{E}[F(\widehat{\mathbf{w}})-F({\mathbf{w}}^{*})]\geq\frac{G^{2}}{128\alpha N},$ where the expectation is over the method’s internal randomness. Arbitrarily many first-order calls between sparse projections are allowed. Consequently, there is a universal constant $c_{0}>0$ such that, whenever $G^{2}/(\alpha\epsilon)$ is sufficiently large, every randomized method that guarantees expected error at most $\epsilon$ on all $s=k=1$ instances requires at least $c_{0}\frac{G^{2}}{\alpha\epsilon\,\log(2G^{2}/(\alpha\epsilon))}$ sparse projections in the worst case.

Remark 2 . As in the deterministic construction of Theorem 2 , the bounded-subgradient property here holds on the entire Euclidean ball containing the feasible set. Indeed, $\mathcal{K}_{\sigma}\subseteq\{{\mathbf{w}}:\left\lVert{\mathbf{w}}\right\rVert\leq R\}$ and, for every $\left\lVert{\mathbf{w}}\right\rVert\leq R$ and every ${\mathbf{g}}\in\partial f({\mathbf{w}})$ , $\left\lVert{\mathbf{g}}\right\rVert\leq\alpha R+\frac{3G}{4}=\frac{G}{4\sqrt{N}}+\frac{3G}{4}\leq G.$ Thus the randomized lower bound also holds under the same type of neighborhood-access assumption discussed after Theorem 2 , and used by MOPES [ 18 ] .

Theorem 6 (The smooth case) . Fix $\alpha,\beta>0$ , let $\kappa:=\beta/\alpha$ , $N:=\left\lfloor(\kappa-2)/32\right\rfloor$ , and suppose that $\kappa\geq 258$ . For every randomized method using at most $\lfloor N/(128\log(2N))\rfloor$ calls to a $1$ -fold sparse-projection oracle, there exists an instance in dimension $n=2N$ with an $\alpha$ -strongly convex and $\beta$ -smooth quadratic objective, a unique vertex minimizer ${\mathbf{w}}^{*}$ , and feasible-set diameter $D\leq 2$ , such that $\mathbb{E}[F(\widehat{\mathbf{w}})-F({\mathbf{w}}^{*})]\geq\frac{\alpha}{8}.$ Consequently, for $\epsilon=\alpha/16$ , every randomized method that guarantees expected error at most $\epsilon$ on all such instances requires $\Omega\left((\beta/\alpha)/\log(2\beta/\alpha)\right)$ calls to the $1$ -fold sparse-projection oracle in the worst case.

Theorem 7 . For any ${\mathbf{x}}_{\rm in}\in\mathop{\mbox{\rm dom}}(\mathcal{R})$ and any integer $T\geq 0$ , let ${\mathbf{x}}_{T}$ denote the output of Algorithm 1 . Then $\displaystyle F({\mathbf{x}}_{T})-F^{*}\leq\left(1-\frac{\alpha}{4\beta}\right)^{T}\bigl(F({\mathbf{x}}_{\rm in})-F^{*}\bigr).$ (21) In particular, Algorithm 1 uses $T$ weak proximal oracle calls and $T$ gradient evaluations.

Remark 3 (use of line-search in Algorithm 1 ) . Algorithm 1 only requires the smoothness parameter $\beta$ in order to set the convex combination parameter when forming the new point ${\mathbf{x}}_{t+1}$ . It is a simple observation that replacing this parameter with exact line-search on the $[0,1]$ interval, i.e., taking ${\mathbf{x}}_{t+1}\leftarrow(1-\eta_{t}){\mathbf{x}}_{t}+\eta_{t}{\mathbf{v}}_{t}$ with $\eta_{t}\leftarrow\argmin_{\eta\in[0,1]}F((1-\eta){\mathbf{x}}_{t}+\eta{\mathbf{v}}_{t})$ , does not change the consequences of Theorem 7 .

Theorem 8 . Algorithm 3 returns $\widehat{\mathbf{x}}\in\mathop{\mbox{\rm dom}}(\mathcal{R})$ with $F(\widehat{\mathbf{x}})-F^{*}\leq\epsilon$ using $\displaystyle O\left(1+\frac{G^{2}}{\alpha\epsilon}+\log\left(1+\log\left(1+\frac{\alpha\Delta_{0}}{G^{2}}\right)\right)\right)$ (32) weak proximal oracle calls and $\displaystyle O\left(\frac{\overline{G}_{0}^{2}}{\alpha\epsilon}+\frac{\overline{G}_{0}^{2}}{G^{2}}\left({1+\log\left(1+\log\left(1+\frac{\alpha\Delta_{0}}{G^{2}}\right)\right)}\right)\right)$ (33) subgradient calls to $f$ .

Remark 4 (The constrained case) . Suppose $\mathcal{R}=I_{\mathcal{K}}$ , where $\mathcal{K}$ is convex and compact, and suppose $\mathcal{K}$ is enclosed by a Euclidean ball $\mathcal{B}$ such that $\left\lVert{\mathbf{g}}\right\rVert\leq G$ for any ${\mathbf{g}}\in\partial f({\mathbf{u}}),{\mathbf{u}}\in\mathcal{B}$ . This matches the assumptions of the projection-based MOPES algorithm [ 18 ] . Then, the additional localized bound $\overline{G}_{0}$ is not needed. Indeed, every weak proximal output belongs to $\mathcal{K}$ , and hence so does the average returned by each invocation of Algorithm 2 . Thus every center ${\mathbf{c}}$ used by Algorithm 3 belongs to $\mathcal{K}\subseteq\mathcal{B}$ . For the auxiliary updates, replace the set $\{{\mathbf{y}}|\left\lVert{\mathbf{y}}-{\mathbf{c}}\right\rVert\leq D\}$ in Algorithm 2 with $\mathcal{Y}:=\{{\mathbf{y}}|\left\lVert{\mathbf{y}}-{\mathbf{c}}\right\rVert\leq D\}\cap\mathcal{B}$ . The proof of Lemma 4 is unchanged. Moreover, all auxiliary first-order queries belong to $\mathcal{B}$ , while the points ${\mathbf{v}}_{\theta}$ used in its proof belong to $\mathcal{K}\subseteq\mathcal{B}$ . Therefore Algorithm 2 may be run with $\overline{G}_{0}=G$ and $K=1$ . Consequently, both the weak-proximal and subgradient complexities are $O\left(1+\frac{G^{2}}{\alpha\epsilon}+\log\left(1+\log\left(1+\frac{\alpha\Delta_{0}}{G^{2}}\right)\right)\right).$

Theorem 9 . Fix $0<\alpha<G$ and $n\geq 2$ , and let $\Delta_{n}:=\left\{{\mathbf{x}}\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{n}:\ \sum_{i=1}^{n}x_{i}=1\right\}$ . Consider the following linear optimization model over $\Delta_{n}$ : at every linear-oracle call, on input ${\mathbf{c}}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}$ , the oracle returns some ${\mathbf{v}}\in\argmin_{{\mathbf{x}}\in\{{\mathbf{e}}_{1},\dots,{\mathbf{e}}_{n}\}}\left\langle{\mathbf{c}},{\mathbf{x}}\right\rangle$ , with any fixed deterministic tie-breaking rule, and after $T$ such calls the method must return a point $\widehat{\mathbf{x}}\in\textrm{conv}\{{\mathbf{v}}_{1},\ldots,{\mathbf{v}}_{T}\}$ . There exists a nonsmooth $\alpha$ -strongly convex objective $f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\to\mathbb{R}$ with unique minimizer ${\mathbf{x}}^{*}\in\Delta_{n}$ , such that every subgradient of $f$ has norm at most $G$ over $\Delta_{n}$ , and for every $1\leq T\leq n$ , every output of such a method satisfies $\displaystyle f(\widehat{\mathbf{x}})-f({\mathbf{x}}^{*})\geq(G-\alpha)\sqrt{\frac{1}{T}-\frac{1}{n}}.$ (37) Consequently, any such method guaranteeing error at most $\epsilon$ must use at least $T\geq\frac{1}{2}\min\left\{n,(G-\alpha)^{2}/\epsilon^{2}\right\}$ linear optimization oracle calls.
